claims.claim: Upregulation of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C in sgDHODH S2-013 cells exposed to nucleoside-free media was reversed by adding back uridine.
claims.source: After 72 hr exposure to nucleoside-free media, sgDHODH cells upregulated HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, and this was reversed by adding back uridine (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from sgDHODH S2-013 cells cultured in nucleoside-free media with or without uridine supplementation.

claims.claim: Treatment with BQ did not further increase MHC-I mRNA expression in sgDHODH S2-013 cells exposed to nucleoside-free media.
claims.source: Importantly, treatment with BQ did not further increase MHC-I mRNA expression (Figure 2E, compare blue and red bars).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from sgDHODH S2-013 cells cultured in nucleoside-free media with or without BQ treatment.

claims.claim: BQ-mediated APP induction is an on-target phenomenon with respect to DHODH inhibition.
claims.source: Together with our other data, these results indicate that BQ-mediated APP induction is an on-target phenomenon with respect to DHODH inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including uridine rescue experiments and genetic deletion of DHODH.

claims.claim: Uridine addback rescued BQ-mediated loss of viability in B16F10 cells.
claims.source: Since uridine addback rescued BQ- and teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability (Figure 2A, S2A), we queried whether BQ-mediated APP induction was caused by pyrimidine depletion per se, or if it was the result of some nonspecific downstream consequence of pyrimidine starvation, such as DNA damage or loss of cell viability.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with BQ with or without uridine supplementation.

claims.claim: Uridine addback rescued teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability in B16F10 cells.
claims.source: Since uridine addback rescued BQ- and teriflunomide-mediated loss of viability (Figure 2A, S2A), we queried whether BQ-mediated APP induction was caused by pyrimidine depletion per se, or if it was the result of some nonspecific downstream consequence of pyrimidine starvation, such as DNA damage or loss of cell viability.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data from B16F10 cells treated with teriflunomide with or without uridine supplementation.

claims.claim: Besides interferon gamma, BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983, the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in the screen of CFPAC-1 cells was mycophenolate.
claims.source: Besides interferon gamma (a positive control), BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983 (another DHODH inhibitor), the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in this assay was mycophenolate, a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from CFPAC-1 cells treated with a panel of chemotherapy agents and small molecule inhibitors.

claims.claim: Mycophenolate is a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
claims.source: Besides interferon gamma (a positive control), BQ, teriflunomide, and GSK983 (another DHODH inhibitor), the only agent that induced APP gene transcription in this assay was mycophenolate, a clinically approved inhibitor of the de novo GTP synthesis enzymes inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IMPDH1/2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mycophenolate's mechanism of action.

claims.claim: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was validated in B16F10 cells.
claims.source: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was subsequently validated in B16F10 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with mycophenolate.

claims.claim: Either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
claims.source: The effect of mycophenolate on APP gene expression was subsequently validated in B16F10 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), demonstrating that either purine or pyrimidine nucleotide depletion can induce cancer cell APP mRNA expression in vitro.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that both DHODH inhibitors (which deplete pyrimidines) and mycophenolate (which depletes purines) induce APP gene expression.

claims.claim: BQ-mediated APP induction in CFPAC-1 cells is not a general phenomenon that occurs downstream of DNA damage or some other response to therapy-induced stress.
claims.source: While we cannot rule out the possibility that these agents induce APP transcription in other cell lines or under other dose/duration conditions, the inertness of these compounds (with respect to APP gene expression) in our screen suggests that BQ-mediated APP induction in CFPAC-1 cells is not a general phenomenon that occurs downstream of DNA damage or some other response to therapy-induced stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that multiple DNA-damaging agents and other stress-inducing compounds did not induce APP gene expression in the screen.

claims.claim: HEK-293T cells display rapid (within 4 hr) transcriptional induction of MHC-I upon BQ treatment.
claims.source: To elucidate the molecular pathway leading to APP induction downstream of pyrimidine depletion, we extended our findings to HEK-293T cells, which also display rapid (within 4 hr) transcriptional induction of MHC-I upon BQ treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ for various durations.

claims.claim: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor) (Thomson et al., 2019), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) (Podolin et al., 2005) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A), despite blocking APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) as expected.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with various pathway inhibitors.

claims.claim: Ruxolitinib, GSK8612, and TPCA-1 blocked APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma in B16F10 cells as expected.
claims.source: Neither ruxolitinib (a JAK1/2 inhibitor with activity against STAT3) nor GSK8612 (a TBK1 inhibitor) (Thomson et al., 2019), nor TPCA-1 (an IKK2 inhibitor) (Podolin et al., 2005) abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A), despite blocking APP induction downstream of poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) as expected.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from B16F10 cells treated with poly(dA:dT) or interferon gamma in combination with pathway inhibitors.

claims.claim: Canonical regulators of MHC/APP expression (IFN-JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and cGAS-STING-TBK1) are dispensable for APP induction downstream of DHODH inhibition.
claims.source: This indicates that these canonical regulators of MHC/APP expression are dispensable for APP induction downstream of DHODH inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that inhibitors of these pathways do not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claims.claim: The IKK2 inhibitor BMS-345541 mostly abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the IKK2 inhibitor BMS-345541 (Burke et al., 2003) mostly abrogated BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claims.claim: BMS-345541 effectively blocked BQ- and Ter-mediated APP induction at concentrations of 10 µM and 40 µM, but not 2.5 µM in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: BMS-345541 effectively blocked BQ- and Ter-mediated APP induction at concentrations of 10 µM and 40 µM, but not 2.5 µM (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ or teriflunomide in combination with various concentrations of BMS-345541.

claims.claim: The effect of BMS-345541 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction was confirmed in B16F10, CFPAC-1, and HCT116 cells.
claims.source: The effect of BMS-345541 was confirmed in B16F10 (Figure 3C), CFPAC-1 (Figure 3D), and HCT116 (Figure 3E) cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from multiple cancer cell lines treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claims.claim: BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I.
claims.source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ.

claims.claim: BQ-mediated increase in cell surface MHC-I expression in HCT116 cells could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541.
claims.source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with uridine or BMS-345541.

claims.claim: Neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression in HCT116 cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, BQ treatment (24 hr) of HCT116 cells caused increased cell surface expression of MHC-I, which could be reversed by either uridine supplementation or by treatment with BMS-345541; neither uridine nor BMS-345541 alone affected cell surface MHC-I expression (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from HCT116 cells treated with uridine or BMS-345541 alone.

claims.claim: TPCA-1 is an established IKK2 inhibitor.
claims.source: Given that TPCA-1 (an established IKK2 inhibitor; Podolin et al., 2005) did not block BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A and C), we suspected that this effect of BMS-345541 was independent of IKK2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study characterizing TPCA-1.

claims.claim: The effect of BMS-345541 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of IKK2.
claims.source: Given that TPCA-1 (an established IKK2 inhibitor; Podolin et al., 2005) did not block BQ-mediated APP induction (Figure 3A and C), we suspected that this effect of BMS-345541 was independent of IKK2.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TPCA-1, another IKK2 inhibitor, did not block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claims.claim: Increased APP mRNA expression was observed upon BQ, teriflunomide, or GSK983 treatment of either wild-type or IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells.
claims.source: Increased APP mRNA expression was observed upon BQ, teriflunomide, or GSK983 treatment (all DHODH inhibitors) of either wild-type or IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from wild-type and IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with DHODH inhibitors.

claims.claim: TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 expression in wild-type MiaPaCa2 cells, but not in IKK2-KO cells.
claims.source: However, while TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha (Yeo et al., 2020) expression in wild-type cells, this was not observed in IKK2-KO cells, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, far right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from wild-type and IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with TNF-alpha.

claims.claim: CCL5 is a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha.
claims.source: However, while TNF-alpha stimulation induced APP and CCL5 a canonical NF-κB target gene downstream of TNF-alpha (Yeo et al., 2020) expression in wild-type cells, this was not observed in IKK2-KO cells, as expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, far right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claims.claim: BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells was significantly reversed with concurrent BMS-345541 treatment.
claims.source: Finally, BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO cells was significantly reversed with concurrent BMS-345541 treatment (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from IKK2-KO MiaPaCa2 cells treated with BQ in combination with BMS-345541.

claims.claim: IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction.
claims.source: Together, these results demonstrate that IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction and that the observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 is independent of IKK2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that BQ induces APP genes in IKK2-KO cells and that BMS-345541 blocks this induction in IKK2-KO cells.

claims.claim: The observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 on BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of IKK2.
claims.source: Together, these results demonstrate that IKK2 is dispensable for BQ-mediated APP induction and that the observed reversal effect of BMS-345541 is independent of IKK2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that BMS-345541 blocks BQ-mediated APP induction in IKK2-KO cells.

claims.claim: BMS-345541 reproducibly bound more than 20 kinases in cell-free KINOMEscan assays, with dissociation constants (kd) ranging from 130 to 8100 nM.
claims.source: BMS-345541 reproducibly bound more than 20 kinases, with dissociation constants (kd) ranging from 130 to 8100 nM (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by publicly available KINOMEscan data.

claims.claim: One potential target of BMS-345541 that met the selection criteria was CDK9.
claims.source: One potential target that met the selection criteria was CDK9, which together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of KINOMEscan data and selection criteria for potential targets.

claims.claim: CDK9 together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
claims.source: One potential target that met the selection criteria was CDK9, which together with cyclin T1 or T2 forms positive transcription elongation factor B (P-TEFb).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the composition of P-TEFb.

claims.claim: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation.
claims.source: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation and therefore is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters (Price, 2000; Ni et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on P-TEFb function.

claims.claim: P-TEFb is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters.
claims.source: P-TEFb is required for the release of promoter-proximal paused RNA polymerase II (Pol II) into productive elongation and therefore is essential for Pol II transcription from paused promoters (Price, 2000; Ni et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on P-TEFb function.

claims.claim: The potent P-TEFb inhibitor flavopiridol phenocopied BMS-345541 by blocking APP induction downstream of DHODH, IMPDH1/2, or CTP synthase inhibition.
claims.source: The potent P-TEFb inhibitor flavopiridol (Chao et al., 2000) phenocopied BMS-345541 in our assays as it blocked APP induction downstream of DHODH, IMPDH1/2 (by mycophenolate), or CTP synthase (by 3-deazauridine McPartland et al., 1974) inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with nucleotide synthesis inhibitors in combination with flavopiridol.

claims.claim: APP induction downstream of nucleotide starvation requires P-TEFb-mediated paused Pol II release.
claims.source: This suggests that APP induction downstream of nucleotide starvation requires P-TEFb-mediated paused Pol II release.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that P-TEFb inhibitors block APP induction by nucleotide synthesis inhibitors.

claims.claim: The BMS-345541 effect of reversing BQ-induced APP upregulation is due to P-TEFb inhibition.
claims.source: It also suggests that the BMS-345541 effect of reversing BQ-induced APP upregulation is due to P-TEFb inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that flavopiridol, a P-TEFb inhibitor, phenocopies BMS-345541.

claims.claim: Two other CDK9 inhibitors (AT7519 and dinaciclib) phenocopied flavopiridol in blocking BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: To further probe whether the observed effect of flavopiridol was due to CDK9 inhibition, we tested two other CDK9 inhibitors (AT7519 and dinaciclib). Both CDK9 inhibitors phenocopied flavopiridol in our assays (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with various CDK9 inhibitors.

claims.claim: A CDK9-targeted PROTAC (PROTAC2) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, a previously characterized CDK9-targeted proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC), termed PROTAC2 (King et al., 2021), had the same effect (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ in combination with PROTAC2.

claims.claim: PROTAC2 consists of a CDK9-binding aminopyrazole warhead conjugated to pomalidomide, which recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cereblon (CRBN).
claims.source: PROTAC2 consists of a CDK9-binding aminopyrazole warhead conjugated to pomalidomide, which recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cereblon (CRBN).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claims.claim: Cereblon ubiquitinates CDK9, resulting in its proteasomal degradation when recruited by PROTAC2.
claims.source: Cereblon in turn ubiquitinates CDK9, resulting in its proteasomal degradation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the known mechanism of action of PROTACs and the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claims.claim: Co-treatment of HEK-293T cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation.
claims.source: Co-treatment of HEK-293 cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation, as free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding (King et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claims.claim: Free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding.
claims.source: Co-treatment of HEK-293 cells with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide prevents PROTAC2-mediated CDK9 degradation, as free pomalidomide competes with PROTAC2 for Cereblon binding (King et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the published characterization of PROTAC2.

claims.claim: PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM).
claims.source: We observed that PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM); however, when we increased the concentration of PROTAC2 to 10 µM (so that PROTAC2 and pomalidomide concentrations were equal), pomalidomide no longer had this effect (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ, PROTAC2, and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claims.claim: When PROTAC2 concentration was increased to 10 µM (equal to pomalidomide concentration), pomalidomide no longer reversed the effect of PROTAC2 on blocking BQ-mediated APP induction in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: We observed that PROTAC2 (1 µM) blocked BQ-mediated APP induction, and this effect was reversed by co-treatment with tenfold excess pomalidomide (10 µM); however, when we increased the concentration of PROTAC2 to 10 µM (so that PROTAC2 and pomalidomide concentrations were equal), pomalidomide no longer had this effect (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HEK-293T cells treated with BQ, PROTAC2, and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claims.claim: Immunoblot analysis showed that 10 µM pomalidomide prevents CDK9 degradation upon 1 µM but not 10 µM PROTAC2 treatment in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: Consistently, immunoblot analysis showed that 10 µM pomalidomide prevents CDK9 degradation upon 1 µM but not 10 µM PROTAC2 treatment (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from HEK-293T cells treated with PROTAC2 and pomalidomide at various concentrations.

claims.claim: All CDK9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction in HCT116 cells.
claims.source: When we repeated the experiment shown in Figure 4B with HCT116 cells, we found that all CKD9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction, but PROTAC2 did not (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with various CDK9 inhibitors.

claims.claim: PROTAC2 did not reverse BQ-mediated APP induction in HCT116 cells.
claims.source: When we repeated the experiment shown in Figure 4B with HCT116 cells, we found that all CKD9 inhibitors reversed BQ-mediated APP induction, but PROTAC2 did not (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data from HCT116 cells treated with BQ in combination with PROTAC2.

claims.claim: Immunoblot analysis showed that PROTAC2 did not cause CDK9 depletion in HCT116 cells.
claims.source: Concordantly, immunoblot analysis showed that PROTAC2 did not cause CDK9 depletion in HCT116 cells treated in parallel (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from HCT116 cells treated with PROTAC2.

claims.claim: CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 on BQ-mediated APP induction.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 and that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that PROTAC2 only blocks BQ-mediated APP induction when it successfully degrades CDK9.

claims.claim: CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that CDK9 degradation is necessary for the reversal effect of PROTAC2 and that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that multiple CDK9 inhibitors and CDK9 degradation block BQ-mediated APP induction.

claims.claim: The dependence of BQ-mediated APP induction on CDK9 strongly suggests that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes, as opposed to increased mRNA stability.
claims.source: The dependence of BQ-mediated APP induction on CDK9 strongly suggests that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes, as opposed to increased mRNA stability.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the known role of CDK9 in transcription and the observation that CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.

claims.claim: The rapid buildup of APP transcripts following DHODH inhibitor treatment (within 4 hr) supports that nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription of APP genes.
claims.source: This is further supported by the rapid buildup of APP transcripts following DHODH inhibitor treatment (within 4 hr, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing rapid increase in APP transcripts after DHODH inhibitor treatment.

claims.claim: ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes.
claims.source: Additionally, ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells (Tan et al., 2016) shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes, and fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression under the same conditions (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells.
claims.source: Additionally, ChIP-seq analysis of global Pol II occupancy following 48 hr teriflunomide treatment in A375 cells (Tan et al., 2016) shows increased Pol II occupancy across many APP genes, and fold change in Pol II occupancy significantly correlated with fold change in mRNA expression under the same conditions (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data from A375 cells treated with teriflunomide.

claims.claim: Nucleotide starvation induces an antigen presentation gene expression program that is independent of canonical APP regulators but depends on CDK9/P-TEFb.
claims.source: Overall, these results show that nucleotide starvation induces an antigen presentation gene expression program that is independent of canonical APP regulators but depends on CDK9/P-TEFb.

results.result: DHODH inhibition by BQ or teriflunomide induces upregulation of antigen presentation pathway (APP) genes and MHC-I transcripts across diverse cancer cell lines in a dose- and duration-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 collectively demonstrate robust transcriptional upregulation of APP genes across multiple cell lines (S2-013, CFPAC-1, B16F10, and various human cancer lines) using complementary approaches (RNA-seq, GSEA, RT-qPCR). The dose- and duration-dependent effects are well-documented, and the findings are corroborated by publicly available data from A375 cells treated with teriflunomide (C7). The smaller effect size in S2-013 cells (C5) is appropriately explained by their resistance to DHODH inhibition.

results.result: Transcriptional upregulation of APP genes by DHODH inhibition results in increased cell surface MHC-I expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 demonstrate that the observed transcriptional changes translate to functional protein expression at the cell surface. Flow cytometry data from both CFPAC-1 and B16F10 cells show marked increases in cell surface MHC-I following BQ treatment. The correlation between mRNA upregulation and protein expression provides strong evidence for functional consequences of the transcriptional changes.

results.result: BQ treatment causes on-target DHODH inhibition, resulting in accumulation of upstream metabolites and depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides, which correlates with APP gene induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 provide metabolomic evidence confirming on-target DHODH inhibition. The rapid (8 hr) and dose-dependent accumulation of dihydroorotate and N-carbamoyl-aspartate, coupled with depletion of UTP and CTP, demonstrates specific inhibition of the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway. The correlation with APP gene upregulation and MHC-I expression establishes a mechanistic link between pyrimidine depletion and antigen presentation.

results.result: DHODH inhibitor-mediated APP induction is strictly dependent on pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, as demonstrated by uridine rescue experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C31 provide compelling evidence that APP induction is specifically caused by pyrimidine depletion. Uridine supplementation rescues both cell viability and pyrimidine levels while completely blocking APP gene induction at both mRNA and protein levels across multiple cell lines (B16F10, HCT116). The specificity is demonstrated by the lack of effect of uridine alone (C26, C30), establishing pyrimidine depletion as the causal mechanism.

results.result: Genetic deletion of DHODH recapitulates the APP induction phenotype, confirming that BQ-mediated effects are on-target with respect to DHODH inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 provide genetic validation of the pharmacological findings. DHODH knockout cells (sgDHODH) show APP gene upregulation when cultured in nucleoside-free media, which is reversed by uridine supplementation. Critically, BQ treatment does not further increase MHC-I expression in these cells (C36), demonstrating that the drug effect is entirely attributable to DHODH inhibition rather than off-target effects.

results.result: A screen of chemotherapy agents and small molecule inhibitors reveals that APP induction is specific to nucleotide synthesis inhibitors and not a general stress response.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 demonstrate specificity through a systematic screen showing that only DHODH inhibitors and mycophenolate (an IMPDH inhibitor) induce APP genes, while numerous DNA-damaging agents and other stress-inducing compounds do not. This argues against APP induction being a nonspecific consequence of cellular stress or DNA damage, and suggests that either purine or pyrimidine depletion specifically triggers this response.

results.result: BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of canonical APP regulatory pathways including IFN-JAK-STAT, cGAS-STING-TBK1, and NF-κB.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 demonstrate that inhibitors of canonical APP pathways (ruxolitinib, GSK8612, TPCA-1) do not block BQ-mediated APP induction, despite effectively blocking APP induction by poly(dA:dT) and interferon gamma. This establishes that DHODH inhibition activates APP genes through a novel, non-canonical mechanism independent of known regulatory pathways.

results.result: BMS-345541 blocks BQ-mediated APP induction through an IKK2-independent mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C62 demonstrate that BMS-345541 blocks APP induction across multiple cell lines in a dose-dependent manner, but this effect is independent of IKK2. The key evidence is that (1) another IKK2 inhibitor (TPCA-1) does not block APP induction, (2) BQ induces APP genes in IKK2-KO cells, and (3) BMS-345541 blocks APP induction even in IKK2-KO cells. This suggests BMS-345541 acts through an off-target effect unrelated to its known IKK2 inhibitory activity.

results.result: APP induction downstream of nucleotide starvation requires P-TEFb/CDK9 activity, as demonstrated by multiple CDK9 inhibitors and a CDK9-targeted PROTAC.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 establish P-TEFb/CDK9 as the likely off-target of BMS-345541 responsible for blocking APP induction. Multiple independent CDK9 inhibitors (flavopiridol, AT7519, dinaciclib) phenocopy BMS-345541, and a CDK9-targeted PROTAC (PROTAC2) also blocks APP induction. The mechanistic link is supported by KINOMEscan data showing BMS-345541 binds CDK9 with appropriate affinity.

results.result: CDK9 degradation is necessary for PROTAC2-mediated reversal of APP induction, and CDK9 is required for BQ-mediated APP induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C84 provide elegant validation using a CDK9-targeted PROTAC with competition experiments. PROTAC2 blocks APP induction in HEK-293T cells, and this effect is reversed by excess pomalidomide (which prevents CDK9 degradation) in a concentration-dependent manner. Western blot data confirm the correlation between CDK9 degradation and APP blockade. The cell line-specific effects (PROTAC2 works in HEK-293T but not HCT116) correlate with CDK9 degradation efficiency, providing strong evidence that CDK9 activity is required for APP induction.

results.result: Nucleotide starvation induces APP genes through nascent transcription involving P-TEFb-mediated RNA polymerase II elongation control.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 establish the mechanistic basis for APP induction. The dependence on CDK9/P-TEFb, the rapid kinetics (within 4 hr), and ChIP-seq data showing increased Pol II occupancy at APP genes with significant correlation to mRNA expression all support a transcriptional mechanism. This represents a novel pathway linking nucleotide metabolism to antigen presentation through transcriptional elongation control.

results.result: BQ treatment suppresses B16F10 tumor growth in vivo, causes on-target DHODH inhibition with pyrimidine depletion, and induces MHC-I and APP gene expression in tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C104 demonstrate that the in vitro findings translate to an in vivo tumor model. BQ (10 mg/kg daily) markedly suppresses tumor growth and reduces tumor burden. Metabolomics analysis confirms on-target DHODH inhibition with expected metabolite changes, and RT-qPCR shows increased APP gene expression in tumors. The metabolomic separation between treatment groups provides additional validation of the metabolic perturbation.

results.result: Sequential administration of BQ followed by dual immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) significantly enhances survival in the ICB-refractory B16F10 melanoma model, while concurrent administration does not improve survival over BQ monotherapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C112 provide proof-of-concept evidence for therapeutic benefit. BQ monotherapy shows marked survival benefit, which is significantly enhanced by subsequent dual ICB (anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4). Importantly, dual ICB alone shows only marginal benefit, and concurrent BQ plus ICB does not improve survival over BQ alone, suggesting that sequential administration is superior. This represents a major finding with potential clinical implications.

results.result: The study establishes that pyrimidine nucleotide depletion by DHODH inhibition induces APP genes through a P-TEFb-dependent mechanism independent of canonical pathways, and provides proof-of-concept for combination with ICB.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118, C146-C147 represent the authors' summary of their major findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including: (1) demonstration of APP induction across multiple cell lines and in vivo, (2) strict dependence on pyrimidine depletion validated by uridine rescue and genetic deletion, (3) independence from canonical pathways demonstrated by inhibitor studies, (4) requirement for P-TEFb/CDK9 shown by multiple orthogonal approaches, and (5) therapeutic benefit in combination with ICB in a relevant mouse model.

results.result: High expression of MHC-I and APP genes correlates with better survival in melanoma patients.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by analysis of TCGA melanoma patient data showing correlation between high tumor expression of MHC-I, NLRC5, and TAP1 with improved overall survival. This provides clinical relevance for the study's findings, though the analysis is correlative and does not establish causation.

results.result: DHODH inhibition may be particularly relevant for tumors with defective interferon signaling, which confers ICB resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 propose a clinical application based on the finding that BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of interferon signaling. The rationale is supported by the experimental data (C120) and citations showing that interferon pathway defects cause ICB resistance (C121). However, this remains a hypothesis requiring validation in appropriate models with interferon pathway defects.

results.result: The mechanism of pyrimidine depletion-induced APP expression may differ from previously reported mechanisms involving ATM or cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 address discrepancies with prior literature. While previous studies linked pyrimidine depletion to innate immunity through ATM or cGAS-STING-TBK1 pathways, the authors show that inhibitors of these pathways do not block BQ-mediated APP induction in their models. The authors appropriately speculate that multiple redundant mechanisms may exist depending on cellular context, which is a reasonable interpretation of the conflicting data.

results.result: The timing and sequence of nucleotide synthesis inhibitor and immunotherapy administration is important, with sequential administration potentially superior to concurrent treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 discuss implications for treatment scheduling based on the survival data and comparison with a prior study. The observation that sequential BQ followed by ICB is superior to concurrent administration is supported by the experimental data (C106, C108). The authors appropriately note limitations of the prior IMPDH inhibitor study (C139) and suggest that their findings highlight the importance of timing, which is a reasonable interpretation.

results.result: The relationship between nucleotide abundance and MHC/APP gene expression is context-dependent and requires further elucidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C145 acknowledge limitations and discrepancies in the field. The authors note that thymidylate synthase inhibitors did not induce APP genes in their screen, despite a published report showing MHC-I induction in a different cell type. They appropriately speculate about possible explanations (cell line differences, dose/duration, specific inhibitors) and acknowledge that key details remain to be elucidated. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The manuscript includes accurate descriptions of established biological knowledge regarding protein functions and clinical practices.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C24, C41, C59, C65-C67, and C93 represent statements of established biological knowledge (e.g., Nlrc5 as MHC-I coactivator, Tap1 function, P-TEFb composition and function, ICB as first-line melanoma therapy). These are appropriately cited or represent common knowledge in the field and provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: The manuscript appropriately cites prior work to establish context and rationale for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C32-C33, C90-C91, C94, C122-C128 represent citations to prior work establishing: (1) S2-013 cell resistance to DHODH inhibition, (2) properties of DHODH knockout cells, (3) effects of MHC-I upregulation on ICB efficacy, (4) MHC-I as predictor of ICB response, (5) B16F10 refractoriness to ICB, and (6) various agents that increase antigen presentation. These citations appropriately establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study.

results.result: The authors provide speculative interpretations about broader implications and future directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C129, C136-C137, and C148 represent speculative statements about: (1) many anticancer drugs potentially having immunomodulatory properties, (2) cells evolving multiple mechanisms to sense nucleotide shortage, and (3) deeper understanding enabling rational therapy development. While these are reasonable speculations based on the findings, they represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated results and should be clearly identified as such.

results.result: DHODH inhibition by BQ or teriflunomide causes upregulation of antigen presentation pathway (APP) genes and increased cell surface MHC-I expression across diverse cancer cell lines in vitro. This effect is dose- and duration-dependent, with RNA-seq showing enrichment of APP-related gene sets and flow cytometry confirming increased surface MHC-I protein.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the in vitro mechanistic data as 'compelling' and 'solid,' with 'rigorous methodology and validation across multiple cell lines.' The editor states 'the in vitro mechanistic data are compelling' and reviewers note 'a strength of the manuscript is the solid in vitro mechanistic data supported by analysis in multiple cell lines.' No concerns were raised about these core in vitro findings.

results.result: BQ treatment causes on-target DHODH inhibition, evidenced by accumulation of upstream metabolites (dihydroorotate, N-carbamoyl-aspartate) and depletion of pyrimidine nucleotides (UTP, CTP) both in vitro and in vivo in B16F10 tumors. This metabolic perturbation correlates with APP gene upregulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the metabolomics data demonstrating target engagement. One reviewer notes the study 'confirms target engagement in vivo' through metabolomics. The editor acknowledges the link between 'DHODH inhibition and subsequent pyrimidine nucleotide depletion with upregulation of cell surface MHC I.' No concerns were raised about the metabolomics or target engagement data.

results.result: APP gene induction by DHODH inhibitors is strictly dependent on pyrimidine nucleotide depletion, as demonstrated by uridine rescue experiments that block both mRNA upregulation and cell surface MHC-I increases. Genetic deletion of DHODH recapitulates the effect, confirming on-target mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the uridine rescue experiments as demonstrating the mechanism. One reviewer states the effect 'is mediated strictly by pyrimidine depletion' and another notes 'the mechanism of the increased antigen presentation pathway by pyrimidine depletion' as a key finding. The genetic validation with DHODH knockout cells is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: A screen of chemotherapy agents and small molecule inhibitors in CFPAC-1 cells showed that besides DHODH inhibitors and interferon gamma, only mycophenolate (an IMPDH1/2 inhibitor) induced APP gene expression, suggesting nucleotide depletion (purine or pyrimidine) specifically triggers this response rather than general stress or DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the screening data or the conclusion that APP induction is specific to nucleotide depletion rather than general stress. The finding that mycophenolate also induces APP genes is accepted as supporting evidence for the nucleotide depletion mechanism.

results.result: BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of canonical APP regulatory pathways including IFN-JAK-STAT, cGAS-STING-TBK1, and NF-κB, as demonstrated by inhibitor studies showing these pathway inhibitors do not block BQ effects. IKK2 knockout experiments confirm IKK2 is dispensable for the response.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the pathway independence findings. One reviewer specifically notes 'the authors provide evidence that BQ mediated induction of MHC is independent of interferon signaling' and another states the study 'determined that BQ-mediated APP induction is independent of several canonical APP regulatory pathways.' The IKK2 knockout validation is not questioned.

results.result: BQ-mediated APP induction requires CDK9/P-TEFb activity, as demonstrated by multiple CDK9 inhibitors (BMS-345541, flavopiridol, AT7519, dinaciclib) and a CDK9-targeted PROTAC blocking the response. The effect depends on CDK9 degradation/inhibition and suggests P-TEFb-mediated Pol II pause release drives APP gene transcription.
results.evaluation: While reviewers find the pharmacological CDK9 inhibitor data 'convincing,' one reviewer explicitly requests genetic validation: 'the mechanism...was not validated by genetic KD or KO targeting by CDK9/PTEFb pathways' and suggests 'an additional experiment with genetic depletion of CDK9 (CRISPR KO, shRNA, etc) would provide compelling mechanistic confirmation.' The reliance solely on pharmacological tools without genetic validation is identified as a limitation.

results.result: The dependence on CDK9 and rapid kinetics of APP transcript accumulation suggest nucleotide starvation enforces nascent transcription rather than mRNA stabilization. ChIP-seq analysis shows increased Pol II occupancy at APP genes correlates with mRNA expression changes, supporting a transcriptional mechanism.
results.evaluation: One reviewer requests additional validation of the transcriptional mechanism: 'The authors show ChIP-seq tracks from Tan et al. for HLA-B. However...the authors should either show tracks at additional loci, or provide a heatmap of read density across more loci. This would substantiate the mechanistic claim that RNA Pol II occupancy and activity...is the major driver.' The reliance on published ChIP-seq data from a single locus is seen as insufficient.

results.result: BQ monotherapy (10 mg/kg daily IP) markedly suppressed tumor growth and increased APP gene expression in B16F10 tumors in vivo, with metabolomics confirming target engagement and RT-qPCR showing increased MHC-I and Nlrc5 mRNA in tumors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the in vivo efficacy and APP induction data. One reviewer notes 'BQ elicits strong anti-tumor activity in vivo in syngeneic models' and the editor acknowledges 'in vivo evidence for additive effects.' The tumor growth suppression and molecular changes in tumors are not questioned.

results.result: Sequential administration of BQ followed by dual ICB (anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4) significantly enhanced survival in the B16F10 melanoma model compared to BQ alone, while concurrent BQ plus ICB did not improve survival over BQ monotherapy. This suggests sequential dosing may be superior.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers challenge the interpretation and mechanistic basis of the combination data. One reviewer states: 'whether the increased antigen presentation by DHODH inhibition actually contributed to the potentiation of the efficacy of immune-check blockade (ICB) is not directly examined is the limitation of the study.' Another reviewer requests critical experiments: 'depletion of immune cells should reduce the therapeutic efficacy of BQ in vivo...Absent this critical experiment, it is difficult to confidently conclude that induction of antigen presentation is a fundamental component of the in vivo response.' A third reviewer notes 'the Kaplan Meier curves reflect more of an additive response versus a synergistic combination' and questions whether the title claim is supported. The editor concludes 'the in vivo assessments of the functional relevance of this mechanism remain incomplete.'

results.result: BQ-mediated APP induction does not require interferon signaling, which may be relevant for tumors with defective interferon signaling that confer ICB resistance in melanoma patients.
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically requests this discussion point: 'The authors should comment in the discussion on how this strategy may be particularly useful in patients harboring genetic or epigenetic loss of interferon signaling, a known mechanism of ICB resistance.' The independence from interferon signaling is accepted by reviewers as demonstrated by the pathway inhibitor studies.

results.result: Analysis of TCGA melanoma patient data shows that high expression of MHC-I and APP genes (NLRC5, TAP1) correlates with better survival in melanoma patients, for whom ICB is first-line therapy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the TCGA survival correlation analysis. This bioinformatic finding is presented as supporting context for the therapeutic relevance of MHC-I upregulation and is accepted without challenge.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the in vitro APP gene upregulation findings (C1-C9). OpenEval emphasizes dose-dependent effects and cross-validation across cell lines. Peer reviewers describe the in vitro mechanistic data as 'compelling' and 'solid' with no concerns raised. Both also address MHC-I protein expression (C10-C12 in OpenEval, included in peer R1).

OpenEval R2 focuses specifically on MHC-I protein expression (C10-C12), while peer R1 includes these claims as part of their broader acceptance of in vitro findings. Both evaluations support the translation from mRNA to functional protein expression.

Both support the metabolomic evidence for DHODH inhibition (C13-C16). OpenEval emphasizes the rapid kinetics and dose-dependence. Peer reviewers accept the metabolomics data and confirm target engagement both in vitro and in vivo (including C98-C103).

Both strongly support the uridine rescue experiments demonstrating pyrimidine depletion as the causal mechanism (C17-C31). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of specificity across cell lines. Peer reviewers accept that the effect 'is mediated strictly by pyrimidine depletion' and also include genetic validation with DHODH knockout cells (C34-C37).

OpenEval R5 focuses on genetic validation with DHODH knockout cells (C32-C37). Peer R3 includes these claims as part of their broader acceptance of the pyrimidine depletion mechanism, noting the genetic validation is not questioned.

Perfect agreement on the specificity screen (C40-C44). Both support the finding that only nucleotide synthesis inhibitors induce APP genes, arguing against nonspecific stress responses. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Both support the independence from canonical APP pathways (C46-C48). OpenEval emphasizes this establishes a novel mechanism. Peer reviewers accept the pathway independence findings and specifically note the evidence for interferon signaling independence, also including IKK2 knockout validation (C55-C62).

OpenEval R8 addresses BMS-345541 and IKK2 independence (C49-C62). Peer R5 includes the IKK2 knockout validation claims as part of their acceptance of pathway independence findings. Both support these conclusions without concerns.

Both address CDK9/P-TEFb involvement (C63-C72), but with different levels of certainty. OpenEval finds the pharmacological evidence compelling and sufficient. Peer reviewers find it 'convincing' but explicitly request genetic validation (CRISPR KO, shRNA), identifying reliance solely on pharmacological tools as a limitation.

OpenEval R10 provides detailed support for CDK9 requirement using PROTAC validation (C73-C84). Peer R6 includes these claims but still requests additional genetic validation beyond the PROTAC approach, suggesting the mechanistic confirmation remains incomplete without direct genetic depletion.

Both address the transcriptional mechanism (C85-C89), but with different levels of certainty. OpenEval finds the ChIP-seq and kinetics data compelling. Peer reviewers request additional validation, noting the reliance on published ChIP-seq data from a single locus (HLA-B) is insufficient and requesting heatmaps across more loci to substantiate the mechanistic claim.

Both support the in vivo tumor growth suppression and metabolomic validation (C95-C104). OpenEval emphasizes the translation of in vitro findings. Peer reviewers accept the efficacy and APP induction data without questioning tumor growth suppression or molecular changes.

OpenEval R12 includes in vivo metabolomics (C98-C103) as part of tumor model validation. Peer R2 accepts these metabolomics data as confirming target engagement in vivo. Both evaluations support this evidence.

Major disagreement on combination therapy interpretation (C105-C112). OpenEval finds proof-of-concept evidence for therapeutic benefit with sequential administration superior to concurrent. Peer reviewers challenge whether APP induction actually contributed to ICB efficacy, request immune cell depletion experiments, note the response appears additive rather than synergistic, and question whether the title claim is supported. Editor concludes in vivo functional assessments remain incomplete.
